title: Chapter 73: The Unruly 2
content:
Chapter 73

That very night, an absolute firestorm erupted.

Midnight struck, and inside the Gilding Pavilion on Koi Tower, nearly fifty clan leaders—major and minor alike—sat clustered around the banquet tables. Jin Guangshan held court from the head seat. Jin Zixuan was currently away, and Jin Zixun lacked the standing for such high-stakes council, leaving Jin Guangyao to stand quietly beside his father with his hands folded at his sides. The front row held the heavy hitters: Nie Mingjue, Jiang Cheng, Lan Xichen, and Lan Wangji—all sect leaders and prominent figures wearing grim, unreadable faces. Behind them sat the secondary clan heads and rank-and-file cultivators, practically radiating paranoid dread, trading hushed, anxious whispers between themselves:"I called it,""Bound to happen sooner or later,""Just wait and see how he cleans up this mess."

Jiang Cheng was the absolute epicenter of the room's suffocating scrutiny. Seated front and center, storm clouds practically rolling off his brow, he sat through Jin Guangyao’s smooth, deferential breakdown just like everyone else:

"...In total, four overseers were slain, and around fifty Wen remnants escaped. Once Wei Wuxian escorted them into the Burial Mounds, he summoned hundreds of fierce corpses to run round-the-clock perimeter patrols around the foot of the mountain. As of now, our scouts haven't been able to advance a single step."

When the report concluded, a dead, suffocating silence fell over the Gilding Pavilion.

It took several heavy seconds before Jiang Cheng finally forced the words out: "What he did was entirely out of line. I offer Sect Leader Jin my deepest apologies on his behalf. If there is any way to make amends, please, name your terms. I will do whatever is in my power to compensate you."

Compensation, however, was the last thing on Jin Guangshan's mind. "Sect Leader Jiang, out of respect for you, the Lanling Jin Clan wouldn't utter a single breath of complaint. But those overseers weren't exclusively our men—several belonged to other allied sects. This makes things... rather complicated."

Jiang Cheng’s scowl deepened. He dug his fingertips hard into his throbbing temple, quietly inhaling a sharp breath. "...My apologies to all the sect leaders present. Many of you may not know the full story, but the Wen cultivator Wei Wuxian went to rescue is named Wen Ning. During the Sunshot Campaign, he and his sister, Wen Qing, did both of us a profound kindness. Because of that debt..."

Nie Mingjue cut in bluntly, "A debt? What kind of debt? Wasn't the Qishan Wen Clan the very butcher that slaughtered the Yunmeng Jiang Clan down to the roots?"

For the past few years, Jiang Cheng had driven himself ragged, working past midnight every single day just to keep his resurrected clan afloat. Tonight had been the first night he’d planned on sleeping early, only to be dragged out of bed by this thunderclap of a disaster and forced to ride breakneck to Koi Tower. Utterly exhausted and already simmering with checked fury, his fierce, unyielding pride was burning under the humiliation of bowing his head in public. Hearing Nie Mingjue casually drag Lotus Pier's massacre back into the daylight, a raw, bitter hatred surged straight through his veins.

A venomous resentment that pointed indiscriminately at every single soul in this room—and squarely at Wei Wuxian.

Lan Xichen mused thoughtfully, "I am reasonably familiar with this Lady Wen Qing's reputation. I don't recall her having a hand in any of the atrocities committed during the Sunshot Campaign."

"She didn't lift a finger to stop them, either," Nie Mingjue snapped.

Lan Xichen said, "Wen Qing was one of Wen Ruohan's personal confidantes. How could she have possibly stopped him?"

Nie Mingjue’s tone was pure winter frost: "Standing by in silence while your clan commits atrocities is functionally no different from holding the knife. You can't gorge yourself on the privileges of an empire while it terrorizes the realm, and then cry innocence and refuse to swallow the bitter pill when the regime collapses."

Lan Xichen held his tongue. He knew better than anyone that Nie Mingjue’s hatred for the Wen dogs was rooted in deep, bloody family grief; the man's moral compass was rigid iron that brooked zero gray areas. Another sect leader piped up in agreement, "Sect Leader Nie hits the nail right on the head! Besides, if Wen Qing was in Wen Ruohan's inner circle, claiming she never had blood on her hands? I don't buy it for a second. Which of those Wen dogs hasn't butchered a few innocent lives? We probably just haven't dug up the bodies yet!"

The second the conversation veered into the Wen Clan's past war crimes, the room caught fire, indignant shouts and heated clamor erupting in waves. Jin Guangshan had been preparing to deliver a calculated speech, and the sudden loss of control clearly annoyed him. Catching the shift in his father’s eyes, Jin Guangyao immediately raised his voice to soothe the room: "Honored guests, please, calm yourselves. That is not the focal point of tonight's council." While he spoke, he gestured for the servants to bring out iced fruit platters to diffuse the room's boiling energy, and the clamor gradually simmered down.

Seizing the lull, Jin Guangshan leaned in. "Sect Leader Jiang, ordinarily, this would be an internal matter of your own house and not my place to pry. But given how things have unfolded, regarding this Wei Ying... I feel compelled to offer you a word of caution."

Jiang Cheng muttered, "Speak your mind, Sect Leader Jin."

"Sect Leader Jiang, Wei Ying is your right-hand man, and you hold him in high regard—we all know this. But looking at it from the other side: does he actually respectyouas his clan leader? That's up in the air. In all my years heading a great sect, I have never once seen a subordinate carry himself with such arrogant, brazen insolence, leaning so heavily on past glories. Haven't you heard the gossip circulating out there? Whispering that the Yunmeng Jiang Clan’s glorious military record during the Sunshot Campaign was carried entirely on Wei Wuxian's shoulders alone! An absolute, utter absurdity!"

Jiang Cheng’s complexion had turned a sickly, bruised shade of pale.

Jin Guangshan shook his head with manufactured pity. "At a prestigious gathering like the Grand Flower Banquet, he dared throw a tantrum right in front of your face, storming off without a second thought! And yesterday, behind your back, he threw caution to the wind entirely—going so far as to brazenly declare,'I couldn't care less about Jiang Wanyin as a clan leader!'Everyone present heard it with their very own ears..."

"He did not," a flat, freezing voice cut in.

Cut off mid-flow, Jin Guangshan froze. Every head in the hall turned toward the speaker.

Lan Wangji sat with immaculate posture, his expression smooth and unyielding. "I never heard Wei Ying speak those words. Nor did I hear him display the slightest shred of disrespect toward Sect Leader Jiang."

Lan Wangji was notoriously sparing with his words; even when engaging in philosophical debates at Great Discussion Conferences, he only ever answered when directly challenged or questioned. He spoke with surgical precision—few words, straight to the throat—effortlessly dismantling the grandest, most winding arguments in a single breath. Outside of that, he practically never voiced an unprompted opinion. For him to cut in now left Jin Guangshan far more stunned than insulted. Still, getting caught red-handed fabricating a lie and stirring the pot in front of forty clan heads was mortifying.

Fortunately for him, Jin Guangyao swooped in to patch the leak before the silence could curdle. "Is that so?" he gasped, wearing an expression of apologetic realization. "Ah, Young Master Wei stormed onto Koi Tower with such overwhelming fury that day, tossing out one earth-shattering remark after another. He likely said something along those lines, and my memory simply conflated it in the chaos."

Jin Guangyao possessed a razor-sharp, photographic memory that rivaled—if not surpassed—Lan Wangji's; Nie Mingjue’s brow twitched with irritation, seeing right through the convenient excuse.

Jin Guangshan eagerly took the out, nodding heavily. "Indeed. Regardless of the exact phrasing, his insufferable arrogance and blatant disrespect remain an undeniable fact."

A nearby sect leader chimed in, "To tell the truth, this has been on my mind for a long time. While Wei Wuxian certainly earned his share of merits during the Sunshot Campaign, there are plenty of guest cultivators who achieved far more, yet not a single one struts around acting like they own the world! To put it bluntly: he's nothing more than the son of a household servant. Where does the son of a servant get off acting so above his station?!"

The moment the phrase"son of a servant"left his lips, several loaded glances darted toward Jin Guangyao standing by the dais—the unacknowledged"son of a whore."Jin Guangyao felt every single venomous stare, yet the warm, polished smile plastered across his face didn't slip by a fraction of a millimeter.

Taking the cue, the rest of the room rushed to pile on:

"Sect Leader Jin demanded Wei Ying hand over the Yin Tiger Tally entirely out of benevolent concern, terrified he wouldn't be able to control such a weapon and bring ruin upon us all! Yet he measures the heart of a gentleman with the petty mind of a scoundrel, assuming everyone is drooling over his dark toy! How laughably absurd—as if our prominent clans lack great ancestral artifacts of our own!"

"I called it from the start: walking the crooked demonic path was bound to rot his mind! Look at him now! The bloodlust is finally breaking out in the open—slaughtering our own men in cold blood over a handful of Wen dogs..."

Just then, a small, cautious voice cut through the clamor: "It... wasn't entirely in cold blood, was it?"

Lan Wangji, who had retreated into an untouchable, meditative trance, subtly shifted his gaze toward the speaker. It was an attractive young woman standing attentively by the side of a clan leader.

Her discordant interjection instantly painted a massive target on her back, drawing venom from the surrounding cultivators: "What do you mean by that?!"

Startled by the backlash, the young maiden shrank slightly, her tone growing even more timid: "N-no... I didn't mean anything by it, there is no need for everyone to get so worked up. I simply feel that the term 'in cold blood' is somewhat inappropriate here."

Another cultivator sprayed spit across the table in outrage: "How is it inappropriate?! Wei Wuxian has been a bloodthirsty slaughterer since the Sunshot Campaign—can you deny that?!"

The maiden fought to stand her ground, stammering, "The Sunshot Campaign was an active war! On a battlefield, does that not make everyone a slaughterer? If we're judging this specific incident on its own merits, I truly don't believe it counts as senseless murder. There was clear cause and effect. If those overseers truly tortured their captives and murdered Wen Ning, this isn't senseless slaughter—it's retribution..."

A cultivator sneered with righteous indignation: "How utterly ridiculous! Are you trying to tell us he had the right to murder our people?! Are you about to praise this as an act of chivalry?!"

Another scoffed dismissively, "Whether those overseers actually did any of that is completely unverified! Nobody saw it with their own eyes!"

"Exactly! The surviving overseers swore on their lives they never laid a finger on the prisoners! Wen Ning lost his footing and fell off the cliff by accident! They even had the decency to gather his bones and give him a proper burial—and this is the vicious retribution they get in return?! It chills the blood!"

The maiden protested, "Of course the surviving overseers would insist he fell! They're terrified of being held accountable for abusing prisoners and committing murder—"

"Save your breath!" a man cut her off with an icy sneer. "We have zero interest in listening to the frantic excuses of someone harboring ulterior motives."

Color flushed the girl’s cheeks. Her voice climbed: "Make yourself clear! What do you mean 'ulterior motives'?!"

The man spat, "You don't need me to spell it out. You know it, and everyone in this room knows it. Just because he flirted with you at the bottom of the Xuanwu Cave all those years ago, you're hopelessly devoted to him? Twisting logic and turning black into white just to defend him even now? Heh, women will be women."

Wei Wuxian’s heroic rescue of a maiden in the depths of the Xuanwu Cave had circulated as juicy romantic gossip for months back then; hearing the context, realization dawned on the room—this young woman was none other thanMianmian.

Snide murmurs rippled outward instantly: "I knew it... No wonder she's crawling out of the woodwork to sing his praises..."

Mianmian trembled with raw indignation. "What do you mean 'twisting logic'?! I am addressing the facts of the situation! What does that have to do with being a woman?! When you can't win an argument with reason, you resort to personal attacks?!"

A cultivator sneered, "Tsk, tsk, look at her playing the pure, innocent victim! Your heart was biased from the start—what 'facts' are there left to talk about?"

"Stop wasting your breath on her. To think our clan actually produced someone like this, letting her crawl into the Gilding Pavilion... Standing beside her makes my skin crawl."

The sharpest barbs being hurled at her came from the very disciples belonging to her own sect. Tears pricked the corners of Mianmian's eyes, her face burning crimson. After an agonizing, suffocating silence, she shouted at the top of her lungs:

"Fine! You're louder, so you win! You have all the reason in the world!"

Gritting her teeth, she tore the clan-embroidered robe right off her shoulders and slammed it onto the table with a deafeningthud, drawing the startled gazes of several front-row clan leaders who hadn't been paying attention. A stunned hush washed over the room—stripping off the robes and slamming them down was the universal, irrevocable declaration ofsevering ties with one's sect.

Without a single word, Mianmian turned on her heel and strode out of the hall.

A beat later, derisive sneers followed her retreating back: "If you've got the guts to strip it off, don't you dare crawl back and put it back on!"

"Who does she think she is...? Leaving is leaving, who cares? Who is she throwing a tantrum for?!"

Scattered jeers chimed in: "Women will be women. Can't handle two sentences of harsh truth. Give her two days and she'll be begging to come back on her knees."

"Obviously. It took her an eternity to crawl her way up from a servant's daughter to an official disciple anyway, haha..."

Leaving the chorus of petty mockery behind him, Lan Wangji rose to his feet and quietly walked out.

Lan Xichen quickly gathered the context of the spat. Hearing the gossip curdling into increasingly vulgar territory, his voice dropped with rare, resonant authority: "Gentlemen. The lady has departed. That is enough."

When Ze-wu-jun laid down the law, the room had no choice but to show him face. The focus of the room smoothly pivoted back to spitting venom at the Wen dogs and Wei Wuxian—an unhinged, black-and-white, unyielding wave of righteous fury consuming the hall.

Seizing the momentum, Jin Guangshan leaned over to Jiang Cheng. "If you ask me, this move to the Burial Mounds was premeditated. Given his monstrous power, setting up his own sect wouldn't be difficult in the slightest. He’s simply using this crisis as an excuse to break away from the Jiang Clan, carving out his own kingdom where he answers to no one. You bled yourself dry rebuilding the Yunmeng Jiang Clan; he was already a walking magnet for controversy, yet rather than keeping his head down, he heaps endless disasters onto your shoulders without sparing a single thought for you."

Jiang Cheng forced his voice to remain level. "That won't happen. Wei Wuxian has been headstrong like this since childhood; even my late father couldn't rein him in."

"Could your father truly not rein him in?" Jin Guangshan chuckled softly, a patronizing rumble in his chest. "Brother Fengmian... simply favored him."

At the wordfavored, the muscle along Jiang Cheng’s jaw gave a sharp, violent twitch.

Jin Guangshan pressed the blade in deeper. "Sect Leader Jiang, you are not your father. The Yunmeng Jiang Clan was only resurrected a few years ago; right now is when you need to establish absolute authority. He doesn't even have the decency to avoid stirring up trouble. If your new disciples see this, what will they think? Are they all supposed to follow his example and treat you like air?"

One barb after another, striking the iron while it was white-hot.

Jiang Cheng spoke with quiet, chilling finality: "Sect Leader Jin need not say another word. I will make a trip to the Burial Mounds myself and resolve this matter."

Satisfied, Jin Guangshan patted his shoulder with heavy, paternal gravity. "Now that is the right attitude. Sect Leader Jiang... there are certain people, and certain things, that simply cannot be coddled."

Once the council adjourned, the clan leaders bustled out into the night, thoroughly energized by the fresh scandal, trading heated commentary as they walked. Behind the sea of white peonies, the Three Zuns convened.

Lan Xichen murmured, "Third Brother, you have had a grueling day."

Jin Guangyao smiled gently. "I'm fine, Er-ge. The real victim today was Sect Leader Jiang’s table—the wood was practically crushed to powder beneath his fingers. He must have been beside himself with fury."

Nie Mingjue strode up, his deep voice carrying an edge: "Pouring out sweet words and oily platitudes—grueling work indeed."

Lan Xichen offered a quiet, neutral smile. Knowing Nie Mingjue never missed an opportunity to lecture him on moral uprightness, Jin Guangyao swallowed his sigh and smoothly deflected: "Ah, Er-ge, where is Wangji? I noticed he slipped away early."

Lan Xichen gestured ahead. Jin Guangyao and Nie Mingjue turned to look.

Framed by the sprawling field of white peonies, Lan Wangji stood facing the young maiden who had just renounced her clan. Tears still glistened in her eyes, while Lan Wangji wore an expression of solemn gravity as they spoke in hushed tones.

A moment later, Lan Wangji lowered his chin, offering her a formal, respectful bow.

A bow steeped not just in courtesy, but in profound reverence. The maiden returned an even deeper salute. Draped in her simple, patternless inner robes, she drifted down the stone steps of Koi Tower, vanishing into the night.

Nie Mingjue grunted, "That woman possesses far more spine than the spineless mob she called a family."

Jin Guangyao smiled warmly. "Indeed."

Two days later, Jiang Cheng arrived in Yiling, leading a retinue of thirty disciples.

At the foot of the Burial Mounds, right before the shattered perimeter wall, hundreds of fierce corpses were wandering the grounds. When Jiang Cheng strode forward, they barely twitched; but the moment his disciples took a step closer, low, guttural snarls rattled in their throats. Ordering his men to hold their positions below, Jiang Cheng hiked up the mountain alone.

He wound through the suffocating, pitch-black woods for a long while before the faint murmur of voices drifted through the trees.

Beside the mountain path sat a cluster of rounded tree stumps—one broad stump serving as a makeshift table, flanked by three smaller ones acting as stools. Wei Wuxian and a woman in crimson robes were perched on two of them, while a handful of honest-looking men were sweating away in the dirt nearby, aggressively turning over the soil with hoes.

Wei Wuxian bounced his knee lazily. "Let's plant potatoes."

The woman shut him down instantly, her tone brooking no argument: "We're planting radishes. Radishes are easy to grow and hard to kill. Potatoes are too delicate."

Wei Wuxian complained, "Radishes taste awful."

Jiang Cheng let out a sharp, irritated scoff.

Wei Wuxian and Wen Qing turned around, neither looking particularly surprised to see him. Wei Wuxian pushed himself up from the stump and walked over without saying a word, tucking his hands behind his back as he continued up the trail. Jiang Cheng didn't ask questions either, falling into step beside him.

Before long, another group of men came into view, bustling around a rough timber frame. They had clearly been cultivators of the Wen Clan, but stripped of their sunburst robes and clad in rough hemp tunics, carrying hammers and saws while hauling timber and straw, they looked no different from ordinary peasants and woodsmen. Catching sight of Jiang Cheng—recognizing him as a great sect leader from his fine robes and spiritual blade—their lingering wariness flared up, freezing in their tracks, watching him with held breath.

Wei Wuxian waved a hand dismissively. "Carry on."

At his word, the men relaxed and got right back to work.

Jiang Cheng frowned. "What is all this?"

"Can't you tell?" Wei Wuxian replied. "Building houses."

"Building houses? Then what were those guys down below doing turning over the dirt? Don't tell me you're actually planning to farm."

"You heard us just fine, didn't you? Yeah, we're farming."

Jiang Cheng’s scowl twisted. "You're farming on a mountain of corpses?! Is anything that grows out of this dirt even edible?!"

"Trust me," Wei Wuxian said lightly. "When you're starving to death, you'll eat whatever's put in front of you."

"Are you seriously planning on hunkering down here long-term?" Jiang Cheng demanded. "Can a human being even survive in this hellhole?!"

"I survived here for three months."

Silence settled over the path, heavy and suffocating.

After a long pause, Jiang Cheng asked quietly, "You aren't coming back to Lotus Pier?"

Wei Wuxian kept his tone deliberately breezy: "Yunmeng and Yiling are practically neighbors. Whenever I feel like visiting, I'll just sneak back for a bit."

Jiang Cheng sneered, "Keep dreaming."

He was about to tear into him further when a sudden weight tugged at his lower leg. Looking down, he found a toddler barely a year or two old clinging tightly to his shin. The little boy tilted his chubby, round face upward, staring up at him with massive, wide black eyes.

Fair-skinned, chubby, and undeniably adorable—it was a darling kid. Too bad Jiang Cheng didn't possess a single empathetic bone in his body.

He glared down at Wei Wuxian. "Whose brat is this? Get it off me."

Wei Wuxian bent down, scooping the little boy up to balance him casually on his hip. "‘Get it off’? Watch your mouth, Jiang Cheng, it's a person. And you—A-Yuan! What's with you hugging everyone's legs the second you see them? Shoo! Hey, don't chew on your fingernails right after digging in the dirt! Do you have any clue what's in this mud? Hands off! And don't touch my face either. Where's your granny?"

A frail, elderly woman with thinning white hair came hobbling over as fast as her rickety wooden cane could carry her. Catching sight of Jiang Cheng's fine silks, she clearly pegged him as a high-ranking lord. Trembling with fear, she shrank into herself, her already crooked frame stooping even lower.

Wei Wuxian gently set the boy by her knees. "Go on, buddy. Play over there."

The old woman hurriedly limped away, dragging her little grandson along by the hand. The toddler stumbled over his own feet, craning his neck back to sneak curious peeks at them the entire time.

Jiang Cheng watched them leave, sneering with open contempt. "The clan leaders honestly thought you rallied some ruthless army of die-hard rebels to play warlord in the mountains. Turns out it's just a bunch of helpless bums, broken old women, and snot-nosed kids."

Wei Wuxian offered a dry, self-deprecating smirk.

Jiang Cheng cut to the chase. "Where's Wen Ning?"

"What made you think of him all of a sudden?"

Jiang Cheng’s tone iced over. "I've had countless people breathing down my neck asking about him for days. Who the hell am I supposed to ask? You're the only one holding the leash."

Wei Wuxian tipped his chin forward, gesturing for him to follow. Side by side, they trudged along the path until a blast of bone-chilling air rolled over them, heralding a cavernous, yawning cave. Stepping past the threshold, Jiang Cheng hadn't taken ten paces in a straight line before his boot caught on something metallic. Looking down, he scuffed a half-broken bronze disc across the stone.

"Hey, don't kick that!" Wei Wuxian snapped, lunging forward. "I'm not done tinkering with it. It’s useful!"

He scooped the battered Compass of Evil off the ground, but before he could dust it off, Jiang Cheng trampled straight onto another item. It was a crumpled, ink-smeared scrap of silk.

Wei Wuxian hissed, "Watch your step! That's important too—I'm almost finished refining it!"

"Maybe if you didn't leave your crap strewn everywhere, people wouldn't step on it," Jiang Cheng fired back. "You've got no one to blame but yourself."

Wei Wuxian grunted, "I live alone here. So what if I make a little mess?"

Pushing deeper into the gloom, the clutter devolved into pure madness. Paper talismans blanketed the interior—slapped onto rock walls, trampled underfoot, crumpled into balls, shredded into confetti—looking as though an unhinged madman had thrown a violent fit in the dark. The further they went, the worse it got, the sheer chaos practically giving Jiang Cheng an aneurysm.

"If you ever dared pull this sloppy bullshit at Lotus Pier," Jiang Cheng gritted out, "I’d light a torch and incinerate every damn scrap you own!"

Reaching the main cavern, a figure lay completely prone on the cold rock. Paper wards sealed him from head to toe, leaving not an inch of skin exposed save for a pair of lifeless, milky-white eyes. It was Wen Ning.

Jiang Cheng cast a disgusted sweep over the room. "You actually live in this hole? Where do you even sleep?"

Tossing his salvaged junk into a corner, Wei Wuxian pointed toward a crumpled pile of scratchy blankets shoved against the far wall. "Wrap myself up and crash wherever. I can sleep anywhere."

Jiang Cheng visibly gave up on pursuing that line of questioning. Crossing his arms, he stared down at the motionless corpse. "What’s wrong with him?"

"He was a little rowdy," Wei Wuxian replied casually. "Didn't want him tearing things up, so I pinned him down to keep him still for a bit."

Jiang Cheng scoffed. "Wasn't he a timid, stuttering coward in life? How does a weakling like that turn so vicious in death?"

The edge in his voice was far from polite. Wei Wuxian cut him a sharp side-eye. "Wen Ning was quiet and cowardly while breathing, sure. But because of that, he bottled everything up inside. Resentment, fury, terror, anxiety, agony—a lifetime of suppressed rot. When he died, that dam broke all at once. You can't even fathom the explosive force behind it. It's the same reason the gentlest people become absolute monsters when they finally snap. The milder they are in life, the more terrifying they turn in the grave."

Jiang Cheng raised a brow. "Haven't you always preached that the fiercer they are, the better? Heavier resentment, deeper hatred, deadlier lethality."

"Usually, yeah," Wei Wuxian admitted. "Except I don't plan on leaving Wen Ning as a brainless weapon."

"Then what the hell are you turning him into?"

Wei Wuxian met his gaze squarely. "I'm going to wake his consciousness up."

Jiang Cheng scoffed with biting derision. "There you go again with your delusional daydreams. Awaken his mind? How would a fierce corpse like that be any different from a living human? Hell, if you can actually pull that off, nobody would bother cultivating the golden core or chasing immortality anymore—they'd just line up to beg you to refine them into walking corpses!"

Wei Wuxian laughed it off. "Tell me about it. It’s a massive pain in the ass. But I already bragged my head off to his sister, and now their whole family thinks I’m a miracle worker. I have to deliver, or where am I supposed to bury my pride...?"

Before the sentence cleared his lungs, the sharp rasp of steel sliced the air. Jiang Cheng drew Sandu in a silver flash, driving the blade straight for Wen Ning’s exposed throat—aiming to sever his head in one clean strike!

Wei Wuxian’s reflexes fired like a coiled viper. Slapping Jiang Cheng’s forearm with concussive force, he deflected the sword's path into empty air.

"What the hell are you doing?!" Wei Wuxian roared.

The shout detonated through the cavern, echoing off the jagged stalactites like rolling thunder. Jiang Cheng didn't sheath his sword.

"What am I doing?" he snarled back, his voice raw with venom. "I was just about to ask you the exact same damn thing! Wei Wuxian, you've been having quite the glorious time throwing your weight around lately, haven't you?!"

Long before Jiang Cheng ever marched up this mountain, Wei Wuxian had known today wouldn't be a friendly, sit-down reunion. From the moment they crossed paths at the foot of the hill, an invisible wire had stretched between them, wound tighter with every breath. They’d traded hollow banter and swallowed their tempers to keep up a fragile facade—and now, that wire had finally snapped.

Wei Wuxian fired back, "If Wen Qing and her people hadn't been backed into a corner with nowhere left to run, you think Iwantedto throw my weight around?!"

"They were backed into a corner?!" Jiang Cheng bellowed. "I’m the one being cornered by you right now! A few days ago on Koi Tower, every single sect leader ganged up to bombard me with demands, breathing down my neck to force an explanation out of the Jiang Clan! You left me with zero choice—I had to drag myself all the way out here!"

"What explanation is there left to give?!" Wei Wuxian demanded. "The slate is already wiped clean! Those overseers beat Wen Ning to death, and when Wen Ning came back, he tore them apart! A life for a life, an eye for an eye! It ends there!"

"Ends there? Like hell it does!" Jiang Cheng spat. "Do you have any idea how many hungry eyes are glued to you right now?! How many wolves are drooling over your Yin Tiger Tally?! The second you handed them an excuse on a silver platter, you threw all reason out the window! In their eyes, you have no ground left to stand on!"

Wei Wuxian scoffed coldly. "You said it yourself—reason doesn't mean shit to them anymore. Trapping myself up here in a cage of my own making is the only move I had left!"

"A move? There's an obvious damn move!" Jiang Cheng pointed Sandu's trembling tip straight at the bound corpse. "The only way to salvage this mess before they mobilize is for us to make a clean break on our own terms!"

Wei Wuxian’s eyes narrowed. "What clean break?"

"Incinerate this corpse right now! Hand the rest of the Wen remnants over! That is the only way to shut their mouths and leave them without a handle against us!"

Jiang Cheng raised the blade again, bracing to plunge it downward, but Wei Wuxian’s hand clamped around his wrist like a vise, arresting the strike mid-air.

"Are you out of your mind?!" Wei Wuxian hissed. "If we throw Wen Qing and her family back into their hands right now, they'll be butchered to the last soul!"

Jiang Cheng roared, "You can barely wash your own hands clean, and you're worried about their survival?! If they get butchered, they get butchered—what the fuck does that have to do with you?!"

Wei Wuxian saw red. "Jiang Cheng! Listen to yourself! Take that back right now before I knock your teeth in! Have you forgotten who helped us cremate Uncle Jiang and Madam Yu's remains?! Have you forgotten who delivered the ashes currently resting in Lotus Pier’s ancestral hall?! When Wen Chao was hunting us like dogs, who took us in and hid us under their own roof?!"

"I'm the one who ought to beat you half to death!" Jiang Cheng snarled, veins pulsing wildly across his throat. "Yes! They helped us! But why can't your thick skull grasp reality?! The Wen Clan is the entire world’s target right now! Carrying that surname is an unforgivable sin, and sheltering them means spitting in the face of the entire realm! Everyone despises the Wen dogs—they want them slaughtered in the most brutal ways imaginable! Protecting them means picking a fight with every living cultivator under heaven! Nobody is going to speak up for them, and nobody is going to stick their neck out for you!"

Wei Wuxian’s voice dropped, quiet and deadly. "I never asked anyone to speak for me."

Jiang Cheng’s patience shattered entirely. "What are you so damn obsessed with?! If you can't bring yourself to butcher them, get out of my way! I'll do it myself!"

Wei Wuxian tightened his iron grip until bone ground against bone. "Jiang Wanyin!"

"Wei Wuxian!" Jiang Cheng barked, his face inches away. "Do you truly not understand how this world works?! When you stand on their side, you're an eccentric genius, a maverick hero, a peerless champion towering above the rest. But the second you sing a different tune, you become a depraved lunatic, an inhuman heretic, a monster defying the natural order! You think you can walk away untainted and live carefree outside their rules?! There is no precedent for that!"

Wei Wuxian shouted back, "Then I will be the precedent!"

Silence crashed down between them. The cavern went dead, neither man yielding an inch, their furious glares locked in a suffocating standoff.

After an agonizing stretch, Jiang Cheng’s voice dropped, laced with bitter, hollow exhaustion. "Wei Wuxian... can you really not read the room? Do I have to spell it out for you in blood? If you insist on protecting them... I won't be able to protect you."

Wei Wuxian didn't hesitate. "Then don't. Cast me out."

Jiang Cheng’s features twisted into an ugly grimace.

"Cast me out," Wei Wuxian repeated, his tone dead even. "Declare to the entire world that I defected. From this day forward, whatever Wei Wuxian does has nothing to do with the Yunmeng Jiang Clan."

Jiang Cheng stammered, horrified, "...For this handful of Wen dogs...?"

His voice cracked, raw with betrayed disbelief. "Wei Wuxian, do you have a hero complex?! Will you literally drop dead if you don't stick your neck out to court disaster?!"

Wei Wuxian held his tongue, staring into the dark.

A moment later, he murmured softly, "Sever the ties now. That way, the fallout won't drag Lotus Pier down with me."

Jiang Cheng stared at him, murmuring in a daze, "...My mother was right. You really are nothing but a curse on our family. She called it."

He let out a jagged, hollow laugh, muttering like a man possessed: "...‘Attempt the impossible’? Fine. You understand the Jiang Clan motto. You understand it far better than I ever will. You all do."

Snapping his wrist, Jiang Cheng slammed Sandu back into its scabbard with a sharp, ringing chime.

His eyes turned cold and vacant. "Then let’s settle it in battle."

Three days later, Jiang Cheng, Sect Leader of the Yunmeng Jiang Clan, challenged Wei Wuxian to a duel. They threw down in Yiling, unleashing an earth-shattering brawl that rocked the entire cultivation world.

Diplomacy failed, and negotiations broke down into absolute carnage. Wei Wuxian unleashed the fierce corpse Wen Ning, whose crushing blow shattered Jiang Cheng's arm. In return, Jiang Cheng ran his sword clean through Wei Wuxian's flank. Both walked away bloodied and broken, coughing up mouthfuls of crimson, trading venomous curses as they parted ways—their brotherhood shattered beyond repair.

In the aftermath, Jiang Cheng made an official proclamation to the four corners of the realm:

Wei Wuxian had defected from his clan, choosing to stand openly against the prominent sects. The Yunmeng Jiang Clan had formally severed all ties and banished him from their ranks forever. From this day forth, the bonds of brotherhood were cut, and whatever atrocities that man committed were entirely his own.
